pages.x: Under the emperor Xuanzong, Tang China was perhaps the richest state on Earth. Its capital, Chang'an, held about a million people, with merchants from Persia, Arabia and Central Asia in its markets, and it was the great age of Chinese poetry.

In 751, far to the west, a Tang army met an Arab army of the Abbasid caliphs by the river Talas, in Central Asia, and lost when its Turkic allies changed sides. China pushed no further west. A story says Chinese prisoners taught papermaking in Samarkand, though paper had probably reached it already.

An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic parents, commanded the armies of the northeast, some 150,000 men. Fat, clever and charming, he won over the emperor and his beloved consort, Yang Guifei. In the winter of 755 he turned his armies on the capitals.

In 756 the rebels took Luoyang and broke through to Chang'an. The old emperor fled west. At Mawei his own guards mutinied, killed Yang Guifei's cousin, the hated chief minister, and demanded her death too. Xuanzong gave in, and she was strangled. Soon after, he gave up the throne.

Fifty years later the poet Bai Juyi wrote a long poem of the emperor's grief for Yang Guifei. It became one of the best loved poems in Chinese, and her story has been retold ever since in plays, operas and films.

The poet Du Fu was trapped in occupied Chang'an. His poem Spring View begins: the country is broken, but the mountains and rivers remain. He wrote of farmers dragged off to the army and of his own children going hungry, and is honoured as one of China's greatest poets.

An Lushan was murdered by his own son in 757, but the war dragged on until 763, won only with the help of Uyghur horsemen, who plundered Luoyang as their reward. The census fell from 53 million people to 17 million, though many were people the broken government could no longer count.

The Tang lasted another 150 years but never recovered its strength. Generals in the provinces ruled like kings, China pulled back from Central Asia, and it grew warier of foreigners. Many historians see 755 as the great turning point of the Tang.
pts: Talas ended Chinese expansion west in 751
Ended the golden age of the Tang
